endorsements.quote: Hospitals should establish multidisciplinary governance committees to oversee AI deployment, ensuring that risk management, technical documentation, and human oversight are embedded within existing clinical governance and quality assurance frameworks ( 8 , 21 ).
Once governance structures are established, the next critical task is to conduct a thorough inventory and classification of all AI systems in use.

This process extends beyond obvious clinical applications, such as diagnostic imaging or predictive analytics, to include AI within electronic health records (EHRs), administrative workflows, and patient engagement platforms.
Crucially, the FRIA must address the GDPR interface.
Healthcare facilities must conduct “Local Pre-Go-Live Validation”.

Site-specific testing to ensure the AI performs consistently on local hardware, checks to identify if the AI performs as expected in the local environment, and interoperability testing to ensure seamless data flow between the AI and existing EHR or PACS systems.
A critical task for the deployer is to assess the technical documentation provided by the AI system's developer.
This review is not a one-time event and must repeated for substantial software updates ( 23 ).
Training programs must be implemented to ensure that all relevant staff possess the necessary AI literacy to supervise, interpret, and, if necessary, override AI systems.
We recommend as best practice the use of “explainability dashboards” and structured override protocols to mitigate cognitive biases like automation bias.
Oversight personnel must have the authority and technical means to adapt or deactivate the AI system, if necessary.
Effective oversight mechanisms and training must empower clinicians to achieve calibrated trust, neither reflexively dismissing the AI nor blindly accepting its outputs.
This involves updating consent forms, patient information leaflets, and staff training materials to reflect the presence and role of AI in clinical workflows.
Once identified, each high-risk AI system must be integrated into a formal risk management process, with clear documentation and accountability structures.
Cybersecurity is a critical component of risk assessment, with the Act requiring technical and organizational measures to prevent unauthorized access, data breaches, and adversarial attacks.
Healthcare facilities must identify a lawful basis (typically Art. 6 and Art. 9 GDPR) for processing sensitive health data through the AI.
Each system must be evaluated against the definitions and risk categories set out in the EU AI Act.

Before a contract is signed, the healthcare facility as the deployer has a legal duty to verify that the high-risk AI system is accompanied by a valid EU declaration of conformity and the required technical documentation (Art. 26).

The oncology center establishes a direct reporting channel with the vendor for critical incidents and performance anomalies, ensuring the vendor is promptly informed of issues affecting the AI system in real-world clinical use, aiding in their own post-market surveillance.

unlisted_practices: Establish AI literacy and training programs for staff without delay, ahead of formal enforcement.
Verify that a high-risk AI system has been registered in the EU database by the provider before use.
Mark AI-generated synthetic content, such as automated reports and patient communications, as machine-made.
Maintain robust training records and competence assessments to demonstrate staff AI literacy.
Report serious incidents or malfunctions of high-risk AI to the provider and, where appropriate, to national market surveillance authorities.
Keep comprehensive logs of high-risk AI system operation to support audit and investigation.
Be prepared to provide affected individuals with explanations of AI outputs upon request.

screen.reason: Regulatory analysis and implementation framework providing compliance recommendations and a roadmap for healthcare facilities deploying AI under the EU AI Act.
